title: On the Limits of Quantum Multiparty Simultaneous Communication
authors: Pedro Montealegre, Ivan Rapaport, Jorge Valenzuela
abstract: The Simultaneous Message Passing (SMP) model provides a fundamental framework for comparing classical and quantum communication. For two players, Gavinsky et al. (STOC 2006) established a separation underlying the incomparability of shared randomness and quantum communication: \textsc{Index Coordination} needs $O(\log n)$ public-coin bits but $Ω(n^{1/3})$ bounded-error qubits.   In this work, we establish a multiparty exponential separation through $\operatorname{IC}_{k,n}$, a natural $k$-party generalization of \textsc{Index Coordination}. Public-coin protocols solve it unambiguously with maximum message length $O(\log n)$ bits. In contrast, quantum SMP protocols without shared entanglement or public coins require maximum message length $Ω(n^{1-1/k})$ qubits in the unambiguous regime and $Ω(n^{(k-1)/(k+1)})$ qubits in the bounded-error regime. A classical private-coin protocol matches the unambiguous bound, so quantum communication provides no asymptotic advantage over private randomness in this regime. For fixed error parameters, all constants are independent of $k$, establishing the exponential separation for every integer-valued function $k=k(n)\ge2$, without restricting its growth. Both quantum lower bounds become $Ω(n)$ when $k\ge c\log n$ for any fixed $c>0$, matching the full-input protocol and yielding tight linear complexity in both regimes.   Our results demonstrate that quantum superposition cannot efficiently simulate the coordination afforded by public randomness, extending this separation to arbitrary $k$. To bound success probabilities for multiparty product states, we prove an exact factorization theorem for unambiguous quantum state identification, which may be of independent mathematical interest.
summary: This work rigorously establishes a multipartite exponential separation between classical public randomness and unentangled quantum communication in the SMP model. By generalizing the Index Coordination problem, the authors prove that quantum communication lacks an asymptotic advantage over private randomness in this setting. This demonstrates that quantum superposition cannot efficiently simulate the coordination power of public randomness across multiple parties.
main_problem: The paper establishes a multiparty exponential separation between classical shared randomness (public coins) and unentangled quantum communication in the Simultaneous Message Passing (SMP) model.
main_result: It shows that quantum communication without shared entanglement cannot efficiently simulate the coordination provided by public randomness, yielding strong lower bounds scaling as $\Omega(n^{1-1/k})$ in the unambiguous regime.
method: The authors use generalizations of state identification theorems, leveraging the factorization of orthogonal complements of subspaces in tensor product settings, combined with information-theoretic inequalities like AM-GM.
model_or_system: The analysis is conducted within the Simultaneous Message Passing (SMP) model, generalizing the Index Coordination problem ($	ext{IC}_{k,n}$) to $k$ spatially separated players communicating to a central referee.
key_observables: Message length (in bits or qubits), success probability, and the scaling of lower bounds with the number of players ($k$) and input size ($n$).
important_parameters: The separation holds for arbitrary $k=k(n)\ge2$, and the complexity matches $\Theta(n)$ when $k$ grows sufficiently fast with $n$.
main_assumptions: The quantum communication is restricted to unentangled messages (no shared entanglement) and the analysis focuses on the unambiguous and bounded-error regimes.
paper_structure: The paper builds upon the two-player Index Coordination separation, generalizes it to $k$ parties ($	ext{IC}_{k,n}$), and derives lower bounds by analyzing the factorization of the orthogonal complement of the 'wrong' subspace in the quantum state space.
why_interesting: The results provide fundamental, quantitative limits on how quantum superposition can simulate classical coordination mechanisms, which has implications for quantum cryptography and communication complexity.
